context: structure-led · deck waterproofing and smoke-control ventilation are the life-safety gate

brief.intro: A multi-storey car park is mostly a repetitive concrete structure — typically post-tensioned in-situ decks or precast double-tee units — built floor by floor on a fast, repeatable cycle. Because the building has no comfort-conditioned occupancy, MEP is sparse: the two systems that really matter are car-park ventilation (jet fans or ducted, to clear carbon monoxide and smoke) and deck waterproofing and drainage, both safety- and durability-critical rather than optional finishes. Fire detection and smoke-control commissioning is the life-safety gate that must pass before the structure opens to the public, proved by a cause-and-effect test that links detection directly to fan activation. Revenue and access systems — ANPR, barriers, payment — are added late and are commercial rather than life-safety, but still need clean power and network runs coordinated with the structure. Ramps, deck-to-deck movement joints and waterproofing detailing at every level are the recurring technical risk, far more than any single MEP system.

glossary.plain: Automatic Number Plate Recognition — cameras that read plates for entry, exit or payment.
a ceiling-mounted fan that pushes air across a deck to clear vehicle exhaust or smoke, instead of running ductwork everywhere.
a concrete slab stressed with internal steel tendons after casting, giving long column-free spans with a thin slab.

proving that a specific fire or smoke trigger causes the correct fan, damper and alarm response.
a deliberate gap in the deck that lets concrete expand and contract without cracking the waterproofing.
mechanical ventilation sized to keep carbon-monoxide levels safe from vehicle exhaust in an enclosed deck.

must_get_right: Waterproof and detail every deck-to-deck movement joint and drainage outlet — leaks here are the single most common defect on parking structures.
Fix the ventilation strategy (jet-fan versus ducted) early — it drives ceiling clearance, structural openings and the smoke cause-and-effect design.
Sequence the post-tensioning or precast erection cycle as the true driver of the programme — it is rarely revisited once a deck is stressed or grouted.
Keep revenue and ANPR systems off the life-safety critical path — commission fire and smoke-control first, then add ticketing and payment without blocking handover.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Activities carry durations in working days; the network is calculated (F9) with no artificial constraints beyond contractual milestones. Total float is kept ≥ 0 in the baseline.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: The structure runs a 6-day week matched to the deck erection and stressing cycle (typically a level per week); MEP and fire fit-out follow on a standard 5–6 day week, one or two levels behind; commissioning is aligned to the local authority's inspection and witness windows.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path is the repetitive post-tensioned or precast deck erection cycle — each bay stressed and grouted before the next level can load it — with waterproofing following each completed deck and ventilation/fire rough-in trailing structure by one to two levels. Smoke-control cause-and-effect commissioning is the life-safety gate before the revenue systems are added and the structure can open.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: The ventilation strategy (jet-fan versus ducted) is frozen before ductwork and structural-opening coordination; a single mobilisation; precast supply, where used, is sequenced to match the erection rate; local-authority inspection windows are known in advance.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Crane and erection access for deck units; stressing crews are a specialist, limited resource that sets the erection pace; waterproofing needs dry weather windows to apply and cure; commissioning needs the fire authority inspector's availability.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: any slip in the deck erection rate cascades directly through every trailing trade; waterproofing defects found after handover are costly to rework; smoke cause-and-effect re-test loops are common. Contingency is held before life-safety commissioning and before public opening, not spread across the erection cycle.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
